Novel insight into enhanced recoverability of acidic inhibition to anaerobic 
digestion with nano-bubble water supplementation 
Yujie Fan a, Xiaojing Yang a, Zhongfang Lei b, Yasuhisa Adachi b, Motoyoshi Kobayashi b, 
Zhenya Zhang b, Kazuya Shimizu b,* 
a Graduate School of Life and Environmental Sciences, University of Tsukuba, 1-1-1 Tennodai, Tsukuba, Ibaraki 305-8572, Japan 
b Faculty of Life and Environmental Sciences, University of Tsukuba, 1-1-1 Tennodai, Tsukuba, Ibaraki 305-8572, Japan   
H I G H L I G H T S  
• The acidic inhibition was alleviated under nano-babble water (NBW) addition. 
• Digestion stability under acidic inhibition was improved by adding NBW. 
• CH4 production was enhanced by 12–17% by NBW addition even under acid inhibition. 
• NBW could promote the production/consumption of VFAs even under acidic inhibition. 
• NBW addition increased the maximum CH4 production rate.  
A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Keywords: 
Acidic inhibition 
Anaerobic digestion 
Nano-bubble water 
Digestion stability 
CH4 production 
A B S T R A C T   
Nano-bubble water (NBW) has been proven to be effective in promoting organics utilization and CH4 production 
during anaerobic digestion (AD) process, suggesting its potential in improving the stability of the AD process and 
thereby alleviating acidic inhibition. In this work, the effect of NBW on digestion stability and CH4 production 
was investigated to evaluate the ability of NBW on AD recovery from acidic inhibition. Results showed that NBW 
supplementation increased the total alkalinity (TA) and partial alkalinity (PA), and reduced the ratio of VFA/TA, 
thus maintained the stability of the AD process. Generation/consumption of VFAs was also enhanced with NBW 
supplementation under acidic inhibition with pH values of 5.5, 6.0 and 6.5. The cumulative CH4 production was 
246–257 mL/g-VS in NBW groups, which was 12.1–17.2% higher than the control. Moreover, with NBW sup­
plementation, the maximum CH4 production rate was raised according to the modeling results.   
1. Introduction 
Anaerobic digestion (AD), a biological process, has been used to treat 
solid organic wastes including animal manure due to various advantages 
including biogas and CH4 generation (Zhang et al., 2019). In addition, 
elimination of harmful pathogens provides the added benefit in terms of 
low contamination to the surrounding environment via AD (Ueki et al., 
2018). Therefore, the treatment of organic feedstock by AD is promising 
to produce clean and renewable energy as well as protecting the 
environment. 
Performance of AD system could be influenced by many factors like 
intermediate products, inoculation ratio, total solids (TS) content, 
temperature and initial pH (Cao et al., 2020). pH drop is one of the 
component factors that trigger hindrance of methanogenesis during AD. 
The shift in pH would lead to variation in the dominant microbial 
community and affect the main organic acids products (Zhang et al., 
2015). Low pH during AD is one of the main factors that cause metha­
nogens to inhibit. This is because the minimum pH value for metha­
nogens to maintain high activity needs to be not <6.5 (Wang et al., 
2014). Rapid pH drops in the early stages of AD, ascribed to the accu­
mulation of volatile fatty acids (VFAs) or long-chain fatty acid, would 
result in reduction of biological activity and finally restrict AD process 
(Li et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2015). As reported by previous studies, opti­
mizing the initial pH with additional chemicals (sodium hydroxide or 
hydrochloric acid) would be useful to maintain the stability of AD pro­
cess (Zhai et al., 2015; Lin et al., 2013). Although the addition of

external chemicals is beneficial to the AD process, the addition not only 
increases costs but also environmentally unsound. The additional facil­
ity which is protected for the surrounding environment against harmful 
chemicals is required. New technologies are desired to overcome the 
obstruction of pH drop to AD, maintain digestion stability and CH4 
production meanwhile under abnormal pH conditions (acidic/alkaline 
inhibition conditions) without additional chemicals. 
Nano-bubble water (NBW) which contains enormous nanoscale 
particle bubbles, possesses many specific properties like higher mobility 
and gas solubility superior to ordinary water or deionized water (DW) 
(Liu et al., 2019). Besides, reactive oxygen species (ROSs), including 
singlet oxygen (1O2), superoxide anion radicals (O2•–), and hydroxyl 
radicals (•OH) would be generated during the collapsing of nano- 
bubbles (NBs) (Lyu et al., 2019). Moreover, the numerous ROSs pro­
duced during NBs collapse may promote the hydrolysis of organics, 
especially the hydroxyl radicals with relatively higher redox potential 
and have been confirmed to promote the degradability of various 
recalcitrant organics (Khan et al., 2014). In addition, NBW supplemen­
tation would also improve the mass transferability (Temesgen et al., 
2017). Due to these unique characteristics, NBW has been successfully 
applied in many fields, such as environmental toxicology (Fan et al., 
2020a), functional food (Guo et al., 2020b), construction industry (Kim 
et al., 2020), biofilm (Xiao and Xu, 2020) and agriculture (Zhou et al., 
2020). Most recently, NBW has been demonstrated to be effective in 
promoting CH4 production during AD process (Yang et al., 2019, Fan 
et al., 2020c), which could be ascribed to the enhanced activity of hy­
drolytic and methanogenic bacteria (Wang et al., 2020). Previous 
studies have shown that different kinds of NBW (Air, N2, CO2, or H2) can 
all increase CH4 production in the AD process (Wang et al., 2019, Fan 
et al., 2020b). However, it’s noteworthy that the above studies were 
performed with no inhibition happened during AD, whether NBW is 
beneficial to improve CH4 production and AD stability under acidic in­
hibition is still unknown. Considering the potential of NBW in promoting 
hydrolysis of organics during AD, it would be of great promising in 
facilitating the recovery of AD performance under acidic inhibition. 
Moreover, as an environmentally friendly and cost-effective method 
(easy availability of NBW and no chemical addition), the supplemen­
tation of NBW for acidic inhibition alleviation would be of great pros­
pect in practical application. 
Therefore, the purpose of this work will be threefold: firstly, to study 
the effect of NBW supplementation on the stability of AD performance 
under acidic inhibition conditions, secondly, to evaluate the CH4 pro­
duction of NBW supplementation under acidic inhibition conditions, 
and thirdly, to analyze the possible mechanisms and application po­
tential involved. This study is the first work to investigate the effects of 
NBW supplementation on digestion stability, CH4 production during AD 
process under acidic inhibition. Results of this study is targeting a new 
application of NBW in AD process under acidic inhibition conditions. 
2. Materials and methods 
2.1. Preparation and characterization of NBW 
NBW used in this research was prepared by using a nano-bubble 
generator (HACK FB11, Japan) based on the previous reports (Wang 
et al., 2019). Air in the natural environment was introduced into DW 
through this generator at 20 ± 2 ◦C. NBW was produced by a combi­
nation of rotational flow, pressurized mechanical cyclic, and cavitation. 
Shearing was performed while pressurizing to generate cavitation, and 
then bubbles were generated through a bubbling nozzle (Wang et al., 
2019). After this nano-bubble generator was operated for 20 min, the 
air-NBW was obtained and applied to the AD process in this work. The 
characteristics of air-NBW and DW were tested for the purpose of better 
comparison. The zeta potential of DW and air-NBW was measured by 
using a zeta potential analyzer (Malvern, Nano ZS, United Kingdom). 
The pH of air-NBW and DW was tested by a pH meter (METTLER 
TOLEDO FE20, Switzerland). The nano-bubble size and concentration 
were detected using the nanoparticle tracking analysis method (Mal­
vern, NanoSight LM10, UK). 
2.2. Batch anaerobic fermentation experiments 
2.2.1. Raw materials and inoculum 
In this work, raw pig manure (PM) sampled from a domestic pig farm 
in Tsukuba, Ibaraki, Japan was used as the substrate. After manually 
sorting out impurities such as plastics and small stones, the raw PM was 
placed in a 4 ◦C refrigerator. Meantime, this raw PM was thoroughly 
mixed to ensure uniformity before subsequent AD experiments. Anaer­
obically digested sludge was obtained from a wastewater treatment 
plant in Ibaraki, Japan. The digested sludge was cultivated using 1 L 
Scott Duran bottles with the raw PM (collected from the same pig farm) 
about one month until no biogas production for acclimation of the 
inoculum. Characteristics of PM and inoculum are presented in Table 1 
according to five tests in parallel. 
2.2.2. Batch AD experiments procedures 
The suitable pH level for methanogens ranges from 6.8 to 7.2 (Zhou 
et al., 2016). When the pH level is lower than 5.3, it is not conducive to 
CH4 production (Wu et al., 2010). Therefore, this work simulated the AD 
process under acidic inhibition with pH values of 5.5, 6.0 and 6.5, 
respectively. All batch AD experiments in this work were conducted in 
250 mL Scott Duran bottles. To simulate anaerobic fermentation under 
initial acidic inhibition conditions, 2.0 M HCl or NaOH was added to 
adjust the initial pH value at the beginning of the AD experiments. Six 
groups of reactors (R) were designed: pH in R(6.5 pH)NBW/R(6.5 
pH)Control, R(6.0 pH)NBW/R(6.0 pH)Control and R(5.5 pH)NBW/R(5.5 
pH)Control were adjusted to 6.5, 6.0 and 5.5, respectively. 10 g PM and 
90 g inoculum were loaded in each reactor, additionally, 100 g DW was

added into RControl groups while the same weight of NBW was added into 
RNBW groups at the beginning of the AD experiments. Rubber stoppers 
and aluminum caps were used to seal all reactors after all materials were 
loaded. All reactors were flushed with nitrogen for 3 min and then 
placed in a temperature-controlled incubator to maintain the tempera­
ture at 35 ± 2 ◦C. The digestion duration was 40 days according to the 
preliminary experiments for all reactors and all bottles would be shaken 
for 2 min at a fixed time every day. All experiments were carried out 
triplicate. 
2.2.3. Analytical methods 
The biogas produced from each reactor was determined every two 
days using a gas-tight 60 mL syringe. Gas compositions (CH4 + CO2 +
H2) were measured by a gas chromatograph (GC-8A/TCD, SHIMADZU 
CO., Japan). Volatile solids (VS), TS and total ammonia nitrogen (TAN) 
were measured according to the standard method (APHA, 2012). A pH 
meter (METTLER TOLEDO FE20, Switzerland) was used for determi­
nation of pH value. Before grinding into powder, the raw PM and 
inoculum were dried at 105 ◦C to analyze C, N, H, and S by using an 
elemental analyzer (PerkinElmer 2400 II CHN Elemental Analyzer, 
USA). The concentration of soluble proteins was measured by using the 
Lowry method with bovine serum albumin (BSA) as the standard. Total 
alkalinity (TA), intermediate alkalinity (IA) and partial alkalinity (PA) 
were determined based on a previous report (Sun et al., 2016). Alka­
linity measurements to pH endpoints of 5.75 and 4.3 were applied to 
evaluate AD stability, among which, PA (to pH 5.75) and IA (from pH 
5.75 to 4.3). Soluble total carbon (STC), soluble inorganic carbon (SIC), 
and soluble total organic carbon (STOC) in the filtrate were measured by 
a TOC analyzer (TOC-VCSN, ASI-V autosampler, SHIMADZU CO., 
Japan). The concentration of soluble carbohydrates was measured by 
phenol–sulfuric method with glucose (+) as the standard. The gas 
chromatograph (GC-8A, SHIMADZU CO., Japan) with flame ionization 
detector (FID) and Unisole F-200 30/60 column was used to analyze 
volatile fatty acids (VFAs).

2.5. Statistical analysis 
The mean value ± standard deviation based on three parallel ex­
periments were calculated by using Microsoft Office Excel 2019 for AD 
experiments and NBW characteristics tests. One-way analysis of vari­
ance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post-hoc test was performed to 
evaluate the statistical differences regarding performance indicators. 
The different letters (A, B, C, …) indicate significant difference at the 5% 
level (p < 0.05). In this work, Microsoft Office Excel 2019 and Origin 9.0 
software were used for statistical analysis, and for the analysis of the 
modified Gompertz model. 
3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Performance of AD process 
Alkalinity, including TA, IA and PA can be used as stability indicators 
for AD process (Sun et al., 2019). Among which, PA represents the 
buffering from ammonia and bicarbonate while IA shows the influence 
from VFA (Sun et al., 2016). The changes in TA of all reactors are shown 
in Fig. 1a. Overall, value of TA content varied in different groups and 
followed the order: R(6.5 pH) > R(6.0 pH) > R(5.5 pH). The declined TA 
content in reactors with lower initial pH value could be ascribed to the 
larger amount of acidic substances (2.0 M HCl) addition for pH adjust­
ment. As for the progressing of fermentation, TA content in all reactors 
increased gradually, indicating the recovery of digestion stability. In 
addition, in all the reactors of R(6.5 pH), R(6.0 pH) or R(5.5 pH), 
significantly higher TA content was observed in RNBW than the corre­
sponding RControl on the 4th and 10th day (p < 0.05), indicating that 
under acidic inhibition, the supplementation of NBW could increase the 
total alkalinity (TA) content in the initial stage of AD, which may play an 
important role in the recovery of the stability of the acidic AD system. 
Fig. 1b and Fig. 1c show the content of IA and PA, respectively. The 
IA content experienced a short-term increase and then gradually 
decreased. Since IA is affected by VFAs, the change of IA content is 
related to the content of VFAs. The content of VFAs also experienced a 
short-term increase and then a rapid decrease (Fig. 2), which was 
consistent with the change of IA content. On the contrary, the PA con­
tent gradually increased with the AD process progressed, which indi­
cated that the buffering capacity of ammonia and bicarbonate in all 
reactors increased. It was worth noting that on the 10th day, the PA 
content in RNBW was significantly higher than the corresponding RControl 
(p < 0.05). 
When IA/PA increases suddenly, the buffering capacity of the AD 
system is weakened (Sun et al., 2016). The IA/PA ratio under different 
acidic inhibition conditions is shown in Fig. 1d. The initial IA/PA ratio of 
all reactors was greater than 1.5, indicating that the stability of all re­
actors was low in the initial state. As the AD process progressed, the IA/ 
PA ratio of all reactors was rapidly decreasing, except for R(5.5 
pH)Control. As for R(5.5 pH)Control, it experienced a trend of increasing 
first and then decreasing, which indicated that the stability of R(5.5 
pH)Control first deteriorated and then gradually recovered, while the 
other reactors gradually recovered their stability (Fig. 1d). In addition, 
the IA/PA ratio of RNBW decrease faster than the corresponding RControl, 
especially in R(5.5 pH)NBW. The IA/PA ratio of R(5.5 pH)NBW was 
significantly lower than the corresponding R(5.5 pH)Control on the 10th 
day (p < 0.05). These results indicated that the supplementation of NBW 
was beneficial to the restoration of the acidic AD system. 
VFAs as key intermediate metabolites in AD process are products by 
hydrolysis and acidogenesis. The stability of VFAs represents the bal­
ance between methanogenesis and hydrolysis/acidogenesis (Li et al., 
2015). The VFAs concentrations in all reactors are shown in Fig. 2. The 
VFAs concentrations increased first and then decreased and were lower 
than 600 mg/L after 28 days. On the 4th day, the VFAs concentrations of

(6.0 pH)Control and R(5.5 pH)Control, respectively (p < 0.05). This phe­
nomenon indicated that the supplementation of NBW promote the 
production of VFAs in the hydrolysis-acidification stage. From day 4 to 
day 16, the VFAs concentrations of R(6.5 pH)NBW were significantly 
lower than that of R(6.5 pH)Control (p < 0.05), while the biogas and CH4 
production of R(6.5 pH)NBW were higher than that of R(6.5 pH)Control 
(Fig. 4). Moreover, compared with R(6.5 pH)Control, R(6.5 pH)NBW has 
significantly higher TA content on the 4th and 10th day (p < 0.05), 
which indicated that the lower VFAs concentration of R(6.5 pH)NBW was 
not due to less production but more consumption. Through this work, it 
could be concluded that even under acidic inhibition conditions, the 
supplementation of NBW promote the production and consumption of 
VFAs in the hydrolysis-acidification stage, which was beneficial to the 
subsequent methanation process. 
As an important indicator to evaluate the stability of the AD process, 
the VFA/TA ratio has been applied in the AD system (Chen et al., 2014), 
and a ratio higher than 0.4 indicates the unstable AD process (Adou 
et al., 2020). Fig. 3a shows the VFA/TA ratio with or without NBW 
supplementation under three different acidic inhibition conditions. In 
the initial stage, the VFA/TA ratio of all reactors was greater than 0.7. 
Since R(5.5 pH) was greater than 1.4, the stability of R(5.5 pH) was 
relatively the worst in the initial stage. As the AD process progressed, the 
VFA/TA ratio of all reactors decreased, which was consistent with the 
IA/PA ratio (Fig. 1d). It took the longest time for R(5.5 pH)Control to be 
lower than 0.4, which indicated that the AD system stability of R(5.5 
pH)Control was the worst relative to the other reactors. Moreover, the 
VFA/TA ratio of RNBW was significantly lower than the corresponding 
RControl on the 10th day (p < 0.05), suggesting that supplementation of 
NBW enhanced the recovery of digestion stability. 
The changes of TAN are shown in Fig. 3b. The TAN content of all 
reactors gradually increased during the initial stage of the AD process. 
This may be due to the decomposition of soluble organic nitrogen such 
as protein in the initial stage of AD, which increased the content of 
inorganic nitrogen including ammonia nitrogen. Bi et al. (2020) re­
ported that when the TAN concentration exceeds 3,000 mg/L, the ac­
tivity of methanogens will be affected and the AD process will be 
inhibited, resulting in a decrease in CH4 production. In this work, the 
TAN content in all reactors was <1,000 mg/L (Fig. 3b). Therefore, no 
ammonia inhibition appeared in this study. 
3.2. CH4 production performance 
The cumulative biogas production and cumulative CH4 production of 
all reactors with NBW or DW supplementation under three acidic inhi­
bition conditions are shown in Fig. 4. Overall, the cumulative CH4 and 
biogas yields of RNBW were higher than those of RControl. As for the cu­
mulative biogas production (Fig. 4a), R(6.5 pH)NBW, R(6.0 pH)NBW and R 
(5.5 pH)NBW achieved 380 ± 5, 365 ± 6 and 363 ± 8 mL/g-VS, 
respectively, increasing by 8.5%, 8.2%, and 8.8% in comparison to R(6.5 
pH)Control, R(6.0 pH)Control and R(5.5 pH)Control, respectively. Moreover, 
the cumulative biogas production of RNBW was significantly higher than

(Fig. 4b), R(6.5 pH)NBW, R(6.0 pH)NBW and R(5.5 pH)NBW achieved 257 
± 4, 248 ± 4 and 246 ± 6 mL/g-VS, respectively, corresponding to 
12.1%, 17.2% and 16.8% increase when compared with R(6.5 pH)Control, 
R(6.0 pH)Control and R(5.5 pH)Control, respectively. Similarly, RNBW also 
showed a significantly higher cumulative CH4 yield relative to the cor­
responding RControl (p < 0.05). 
In order to better analyze the kinetics of the AD process of PM with 
NBW or DW supplementation under three different degrees of acidic 
inhibition conditions, the modified Gompertz model was applied and the 
relevant parameters are shown in Table 2. The results showed that the 
experimental data well fitted the modified Gompertz model (R2 = 0.994 
to 0.998). The difference in the lag phase between RControl and RNBW was 
not statistically significant (p > 0.05). However, the Rmax of RNBW was 
significantly larger than the corresponding RControl (p < 0.05), implying 
that NBW supplementation increase the maximum CH4 production rate 
even under acid inhibition conditions. 
3.3. Soluble organics performance 
The changes in soluble proteins and carbohydrates in this work are 
shown in Fig. 5a and Fig. 5b. The soluble proteins in all reactors expe­
rienced a trend of increasing and then decreasing. The initial increase 
may be because hydrolysis promoted the production of soluble proteins, 
and the consumption rate of soluble proteins was slower than produc­
tivity. Regarding the change of soluble proteins on the 4th day, the 
increments of RNBW were faster than those of RControl, but the difference 
was not statistically significant (p > 0.05). With the progress of AD, the 
production rate of soluble proteins was lower than the consumption rate, 
and its content gradually decreased. For the soluble carbohydrates on 
the 4th day, R(6.5 pH)NBW were significantly lower than those of R(6.0 
pH)NBW, R(6.0 pH)Control and R(5.5 pH)NBW (p < 0.05), suggesting that 
with the deepening of acidic inhibition, the consumption rate of soluble 
carbohydrates became slower. 
Fig. 5c showed the changes of soluble TOC in 40 days’ AD with the 
supplementation of NBW or DW under acidic inhibition conditions. 
Obviously, the soluble TOC showed a tendency to increase and then 
decrease. At the beginning of the AD process at day 0, the soluble TOC 
content of all reactors was basically the same. The difference was not 
statistically significant (p > 0.05). As the AD process progressed, on the 
4th day, the soluble TOC content of all reactors increased, which were 
consistent with the changes in VFAs (Fig. 2). Among them, the soluble 
TOC content of R(6.5 pH)NBW was significantly higher than that of R(6.0 
pH) and R(5.5 pH) (p < 0.05). With the progress of AD, the soluble TOC 
content of all reactors gradually decreased. 
The changes in TS and VS content were shown in Fig. 5d. The initial 
TS and VS contents were 21.64 ± 0.38 and 16.71 ± 0.84 g/L, respec­
tively. The difference in the initial TS and VS contents was not statisti­
cally significant (p greater than 0.05). The final VS content of R(6.5 
pH)NBW was significantly lower than that of R(6.0 pH)Control and R(5.5 
pH)Control (p < 0.05). In terms of the VS reduction rate, R(6.5 pH)NBW, R

3.4. Related possible mechanisms and application potential 
In this work, multiple parallel tests indicated that under acidic in­
hibition conditions, the supplementation of NBW would promote CH4 
production (Fig. 4) and digestion stability (Fig. 1 and Fig. 3a) during AD 
processes. To further clarify the related mechanisms, the characteristics 
of NBW and DW were also determined. As shown in Table 3, the zeta 
potential (absolute value) of NBW was significantly higher than DW (p 
< 0.05). As known, zeta potential is an electric potential generated at the 
solid–liquid interface in response to the relative movement of solid 
particles and liquid (Cacua et al., 2019). Zeta potential plays an 
important role in the stability of the bubble (Parmar and Majumder, 
2013). In addition, higher zeta potential may lead to higher moving 
speed, which may also be a reason for the higher mobility of NBW 
(Takahashi, 2005). Therefore, the higher zeta potential of NBW may 
cause high water molecule mobility, thereby enhancing the AD process. 
Moreover, a previous study showed that NBW has higher spin–spin 
relaxation times (T2) compared to DW (Wang et al., 2020). The larger 
the T2, the more susceptible the hydrogen-bonding network is to inter­
ference, thus the higher the mobility of water molecules (Liu et al., 
2013). Therefore, the water molecule mobility of RNBW was higher than 
that of RControl. 
As reported by Wang et al. (2019), hundreds of millions of NBs could 
exist stably in NBW for more than 14 days. Michailidi et al. (2020) re­
ported that the NBs produced have long-term stability, up to three 
months. Moreover, after 35 days, the mobility of NBW was still higher 
than that of DW (Wang et al., 2020). Therefore, compared with RControl, 
the reactors of RNBW were more likely to have high mobility during the 
entire AD process rather than only in a shorter time. Therefore, 
combining the characteristics of NBW and the results of this work, the 
possible mechanisms of NBW supplementation in AD of PM under acidic 
inhibition conditions are shown in Fig. 6. At the beginning of the AD 
process, NBW with higher NBs density, zeta potential (absolute value), 
T2 value, and water molecule mobility than DW was added into the 
reactors. Previous studies have shown that NBW enhances the activity of 
related hydrolases in the hydrolysis stage (Yang et al., 2019, Fan et al., 
2020b). As the fermentation progressed, compared to RControl, the gen­
eration/consumption of VFAs was enhanced in RNBW, which indicated 
that the supplementation of NBW facilitated the alleviation of acidic 
inhibition in the acidification stage. After that, during the methano­
genesis stage, NBW supplementation enhanced the CH4 production in 
the methanogenesis stage. Therefore, the higher water molecule 
mobility due to NBW supplementation enhances the entire AD process 
even under acidic inhibition. 
This work demonstrated that under acidic inhibition conditions, 
NBW still promote CH4 production. In this work, the increase in CH4 
production in the AD of PM was relatively low, ranging from 12.1% to 
17.2%, which was lower than the 21.5% increase achieved by the sup­
plementation of ferrous chloride (Lu et al., 2020) under normal condi­
tions, and also lower than the 36.51% increase achieved by lignite 
supplementation (Guo et al., 2020a) under normal conditions. However, 
it is important that the increase in CH4 production achieved in this work 
was in acidic inhibition conditions, not in normal conditions. When 
NBW was used in the AD process of PM under acidic inhibition condi­
tions, although the supplementation of NBW did not increase the CH4 
production effectively, it promoted the digestion stability and played an 
important role in alleviating acidic inhibition. Moreover, as a pollution- 
free, chemical-free, and low-cost technology, the manufacture of NBW 
did not require complex devices or consume too much energy. With the 
continuous development of NBW technology, NBW may not only 
significantly alleviate acidic inhibition and improve AD system stability, 
but also greatly increase CH4 production in the future. Moreover, the 
application of NBW technology could not only effectively treat acidic 
substrates, but also avoid the use of chemicals, which was conducive to 
reducing the use of chemicals. Therefore, in the AD process under acidic 
inhibition, NBW technology may have huge potential in the future and is 
worthy of further research.

4. Conclusions 
This study investigated the ability of NBW in promoting AD recovery 
from acidic inhibition. Results demonstrated that stability of the AD 
process suffered acidic inhibition was maintained with the NBW sup­
plementation, due to the elevation of TA and PA, as well as the declining 
ratio of VFA/TA. Besides, generation/consumption of VFAs was accel­
erated with NBW supplementation. Moreover, 12.1–17.2% higher cu­
mulative CH4 yield were achieved in NBW groups when compared to the 
corresponding controls. The above results showed an enhanced recov­
erability of NBW-based AD system from acidic inhibition, suggested the 
promising application of NBW for the alleviation of extreme conditions.
